headline: Man found guilty of starting the Palisades Fire

sources.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting 2025 Palisades Fire (NPR)
Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles (BBC)
Man accused of sparking deadly Los Angeles wildfire found guilty (The Guardian)
Man accused of sparking deadly Palisades Fire found guilty of arson (CNN)

chunks.text: On November 20, 2026, a [[jury]] in Los Angeles reached its [[verdict]] in the Palisades Fire case. A jury is a group of ordinary people who decide a [[trial]], a case in court. A verdict is their final decision. The jury found a 30-year-old man [[guilty]] of [[arson]], the crime of starting a fire [[on purpose]]. The January 2025 fire killed 12 people and {{burned down}} more than 6,800 buildings in Los Angeles and Malibu.

verbs.correct: To destroy a building completely with fire
verbs.wrong: To light a building brightly for a party
verbs.why: Wildfires burn down homes in dry places every summer. A candle left alone sometimes burns down a whole house. The January 2025 fire killed 12 people and burned down more than 6,800 buildings.

chunks.text: [[Prosecutors]], the lawyers for the government, said the man started a small fire on a hill on January 1. Firefighters {{put out}} the flames. But the fire kept burning, unseen, in [[plant roots]] underground. On January 7, [[strong winds]] helped it {{break out}} again. He said he was [[innocent]]. His first trial, in June 2026, ended in a [[mistrial]], because the jury could not agree. Ten of the 12 thought he was not guilty.

verbs.correct: To stop a fire from burning
verbs.wrong: To use a fire for cooking food
verbs.why: Firefighters put out most kitchen fires in a few minutes. My dad puts out the campfire with a bucket of water. Firefighters put out the flames of the small fire on January 1, 2025.

verbs.wrong: To become wet in the morning rain
verbs.why: Fires break out often in hot, dry, windy weather. A fire sometimes breaks out when people cook with too much oil. On January 7, 2025, strong winds helped the hidden fire break out again.

chunks.text: Prosecutors did not {{give up}}. At the [[retrial]], a new trial with a new jury, they {{laid out}} their [[evidence]], the facts used to prove a case. Photos showed his car below the hill. [[Cell phone tower]] data {{backed up}} their claim that he was on the hill. Their experts {{ruled out}} other causes, such as fireworks. His lawyer said fireworks may have caused it.

verbs.correct: To stop trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To sing a song in a court
verbs.why: Good students do not give up when a test is hard. She never gives up when her team is losing. Prosecutors did not give up after the first trial ended in a mistrial.

verbs.correct: To explain something clearly in detail
verbs.wrong: To fold something into small squares
verbs.why: A good teacher lays out the plan for the class on the first day. The coach lays out the rules before every game. At the retrial, prosecutors laid out their evidence against the man.

verbs.correct: To show that something is true
verbs.wrong: To send a message to many people
verbs.why: Good reporters back up their stories with facts. Photos often back up what a witness says. Cell phone tower data backed up the prosecutors' claim that the man was on the hill.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To buy something at a low price
verbs.why: Doctors rule out some illnesses with a simple blood test. The police rule out a person when the facts show he was far away. The prosecutors' experts ruled out other causes of the fire, such as fireworks.

chunks.text: On the new jury, only one person first thought the man was not guilty. He {{came around}} after listening to every point. The man's [[sentence]], or [[punishment]], is scheduled for March 17, 2027. Each of his two crimes can mean 5 to 20 years in prison. His lawyer was [[disappointed]] but respected the jury. He said they will {{look into}} their options, including an [[appeal]], which asks a [[higher court]] to review the case. The city's mayor said no verdict can {{bring back}} the lives lost.

verbs.correct: To change your mind and agree
verbs.wrong: To grow a long gray beard
verbs.why: My parents often come around to my ideas after a long talk. He hates new music at first, but he usually comes around. One juror came around after listening to every point.

verbs.wrong: To lock something in a box
verbs.why: The school looks into every complaint from parents. My bank looks into strange charges on my card. The man's lawyer said they will look into all their options, including an appeal.

verbs.correct: To return something that is gone
verbs.wrong: To paint something on a wall
verbs.why: A new phone does not bring back deleted photos. Money never brings back lost time. The city's mayor said no verdict can bring back the lives lost in the fire.

mainIdea.s: A jury found a man guilty of arson for the fire that became the deadly Palisades Fire. Its verdict came at a second trial, because the first jury could not agree on whether he was guilty.
mainIdea.why: The jury found him guilty of arson at the retrial. His first trial ended in a mistrial, but prosecutors did not give up.

mainIdea.s: At his first trial in June 2026, a man was found guilty of setting a huge fire near the coast. A judge then gave him 20 years in prison, and his lawyers have already filed an appeal.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the first trial ended in a mistrial. The guilty verdict came at the retrial, his sentence comes in March 2027, and his lawyers only said they will look into an appeal.

mainIdea.s: Builders in Los Angeles have finished new homes for families who lost houses in the January 2025 wildfires. City officials say thousands of people will return to their neighborhoods by spring.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a court decision. A jury found a man guilty of starting the fire that burned down more than 6,800 buildings.

tf.s: A jury found the man guilty of starting the Palisades Fire.
tf.why: The jury found him guilty of arson. The fire killed 12 people and burned down more than 6,800 buildings.

tf.s: The Palisades Fire was a new fire with no link to the first small fire.
tf.why: It was the same fire. It kept burning in plant roots under the ground and broke out again on January 7.

tf.s: At the first trial, the jury found the man guilty.
tf.why: The first trial ended in a mistrial because the jury could not agree. Prosecutors did not give up, so the case went to a new trial.

tf.s: At the retrial, prosecutors laid out evidence that he was on the hill.
tf.why: Photos showed his car below the hill, and cell phone tower data backed up their claim.

tf.s: The prosecutors' experts said that fireworks started the fire.
tf.why: The prosecutors' experts ruled out other causes, such as fireworks. It was the man's lawyer who said fireworks may have caused it.

tf.s: The man's lawyer said they will look into an appeal and other options.
tf.why: His lawyer was disappointed but respected the jury. An appeal asks a higher court to review the case.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the Palisades Fire trial?
I did. The jury found the man guilty on November 20, right?
Yes. And that was his second trial. The first one ended in a mistrial.
Really? I thought it was an [[open-and-shut case]].
Not at all. Ten of the twelve jurors in the first trial thought he was not guilty. But the prosecutors didn't {{give up}}.
Wait, how did the fire even start?
Prosecutors say he started a small fire on January 1. Firefighters {{put out}} the flames, but it kept burning under the ground.
And then it {{broke out}} again on January 7?
Exactly. At the retrial, the prosecutors {{laid out}} their evidence again. Phone tower data {{backed up}} their claim that he was on the hill.
What about his lawyer's idea about fireworks?
The prosecutors' experts {{ruled out}} fireworks. And one juror had a real [[change of heart]].
At first, he was the only one who thought the man was not guilty. He {{came around}} after hearing every point.
So he gave the man [[the benefit of the doubt]] at first.
Right. A judge is set to decide the sentence in March, and his lawyers say they'll {{look into}} an appeal.
I hope the verdict gives the families [[some closure]].
Maybe a little. The mayor said no verdict can {{bring back}} the people they lost.
And that fire {{burned down}} more than 6,800 buildings. So many people are still trying to rebuild.

expressions.def: Used to say that a case is very easy to decide because the facts seem clear
ex: The police thought it was an open-and-shut case.
It looked like an open-and-shut case, but the trial lasted weeks.

expressions.def: A change in what you think or feel about something
ex: She had a change of heart and took the job after all.

expressions.def: Used when you choose to believe someone because you cannot prove they are wrong
ex: He was late again, but I gave him the benefit of the doubt.

expressions.def: A feeling that a painful time has finally ended
ex: The funeral gave the family some closure.
